One hour before the wedding, the bride was already waiting.
Evelyn stood in her dressing room in a gown of ivory silk, her pulse racing beneath the beading. She couldn't stop smiling. Every few seconds she lifted the bouquet to her face and breathed it in, then turned back to the window and the wide, sunlit garden below.
One more hour, and she would be Damian Blake's wife. One more hour, and she would walk out of a house that had never once chosen her over her sister. One more hour, and there would be nothing left but happiness. One more hour, and twenty years of quiet grief would finally trade themselves for a smile she hoped might last forever.
The lock clicked behind her.
The door opened, and she turned on instinct. Both her parents came in wearing the same tight, careful expressions, and something in Evelyn's chest went cold at the sight of them.
"Evelyn." Her father's voice carried clean across the marble.
"What is it, Dad?"
"There's something I have to tell you," Robert Hart said, his face folding into something she couldn't read.
"Go ahead."
"Today, you will not be marrying Damian Blake."
The words froze her where she stood. Her fingers tightened around the bouquet until the stems bit into her palm.
"What do you mean?"
He exhaled, long and heavy. "Vanessa will marry Damian in your place."
Her heart lurched.
It was as if a thousand invisible hands had reached in and squeezed it all at once — and worse still when she saw her sister sweep into the room, beaming, radiant, wearing a wedding gown far more expensive than her own.
Vanessa smiled wide. There was not a trace of guilt on her face.
"Dad, you can't do this." Evelyn shook her head. "This is my wedding day. Vanessa has no right to tear it apart. And Damian isn't a thing — he isn't a toy you can hand off to whoever you please."
"Damian has already agreed," Robert said flatly.
Her legs nearly gave out under her.
"Damian, come in here! Explain your own mistake to Evelyn yourself," the fifty-five-year-old man commanded.
A moment later a man stepped through the door, striking in his white groom's suit, his head bowed low. Guilt was written all over him.
"Evelyn," Damian said softly.
Her tears came fast and hard. Her heart truly broke — and even before he spoke, she could already guess the shape of it.
Her groom had fallen in love with her own sister. With Vanessa.
"…Vanessa is carrying my child."
"W-what?"
She had known this was a betrayal. She just hadn't imagined it had already gone this far.
"I'm sorry," Damian murmured. "But I have to take responsibility."
"How long have the two of you been sneaking around behind my back?" Evelyn asked, the pieces of her heart caving in further with every word.
"Six months," Vanessa answered, without a shred of remorse. "I'm sorry, Evie. But Damian's just more comfortable with me than he ever was with you."
A growl tore out of Evelyn's throat. Before she knew it, her hand flew and cracked hard across Vanessa's face.
The slap rang out. Vanessa's head snapped to the side.
Then another slap — and this time it was Evelyn's face that whipped sideways, worse than her sister's, the corner of her lip splitting open.
"How dare you raise your hand to your own sister!" Robert roared.
As always, he stood at Vanessa's side, even when Vanessa was the one in the wrong.
"She hurt me first," Evelyn shouted. "She stole the man I was supposed to marry."
"Can't you lower your voice?" Her mother finally spoke up too. "Do you want to drag your sister's good name through the mud?"
Evelyn laughed, an ugly, broken sound. Look at that. How plain their favoritism was, laid bare for anyone to see.
"Her name's already in the mud. She's nothing but a cheap little tramp, and the two of you still take her side," Evelyn spat.
"Vanessa is not a tramp, Evelyn!" Damian snapped. "Watch your mouth. Don't ever let me hear you insult my bride again."
Her body swayed. She almost lost her balance entirely. Was there anything in the world that could put this kind of pain into words?
Once again Vanessa had taken what was hers. Her happiness.
"Fine. If the two of you want to get married, then go ahead." Evelyn ripped the veil from her head. She flung the bouquet to the floor and ground it under her heel until it was nothing but crushed petals.
Quick as lightning, she walked out. Every second longer in that room only made it harder to breathe.
"Where do you think you're going? Get back here, Evelyn!" her father shouted after her.
But Evelyn didn't care. She just kept running.
"Dad, Mom, Damian… I'm so sorry," Vanessa whimpered, her eyes going red. "This is all my fault. Now Evelyn hates all of you because of me."
"It isn't your fault," her mother said. "Evelyn's just immature. She should be able to understand that the baby in your belly needs its father."

Five years passed after that day. And now Evelyn was married to Gavin Lionel Mercer — a man five years her senior, steady and attentive by nature.
Tonight was their fourth wedding anniversary. But like every celebration before it, Gavin hadn't come home.
Evelyn wasn't a fool. She knew exactly where her husband went. She simply chose to pretend she didn't.
Two in the morning. Gavin finally came home. He eased the door open and crept through the dark, aiming to slip upstairs unnoticed.
The lights snapped on.
His foot, already on the second step, went still. He turned — and found his wife sitting in the front room, spine straight, hands folded neatly in her lap, exactly like a doll with the life gone out of it.
"Evelyn," Gavin said, awkward.
"Where have you been?"
The question came out cold. None of the old worry was in it — just a flat, even calm. Gavin didn't notice the difference at all.
"There was an important meeting with a client. I didn't get a chance to let you know. I'm sorry."
He crossed the room toward her and sat down at her side, meaning to press a warm kiss to her forehead.
Instead, she brought a hand up against his chest, stopping him before he could.
"You smell like another woman," Evelyn said. "I don't like it."
Gavin faltered. It was true — his cologne had mixed with the sweet trace of a woman's perfume.
"Sorry. That's probably my secretary's perfume. She bumped into me earlier by accident," he offered.
"You should go shower," Evelyn said.
"All right," Gavin nodded.
"Do you want me to make you something?"
"Mm… chamomile tea, then," he said after a few seconds' thought.
Evelyn nodded. She watched him take the stairs, one step at a time.
"Gavin," she called after him.
"Yes?" He turned. He was halfway up.
She was quiet for a moment. She swallowed hard. Her eyes trembled, just slightly.
"Happy fourth anniversary," Evelyn said.
Silence. Gavin's body went still where he stood. For reasons he couldn't name, he felt as if his wife had become someone he no longer recognized.
